analysis.one_liner: Bans union security agreements, ending mandatory union dues or fees as a job condition nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let workers refuse to pay union dues or fees anywhere in the country, died in the Senate Labor Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current federal law, if a majority of workers at a workplace vote for union representation, the union and employer can agree that employees must join the union or pay fees covering the cost of representing them. This bill would repeal those provisions in two federal labor laws, so no worker anywhere could be required to pay a union as a condition of keeping their job. Supporters called it worker freedom; unions and their allies said it would starve unions of the dues that fund bargaining, since workers could get union representation without paying for it.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees who object to paying union dues or fees — roughly all workers covered by a union contract who choose not to contribute. Employers also gain, because unions with less guaranteed funding bargain with less power, which tends to hold down labor costs. The National Right to Work Committee and similar employer-backed groups promoted exactly this policy.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sections of the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act that let a union and employer agree that workers must join the union or pay dues or fees to keep their job [S2][S3].
Also repeals the provision allowing railroads to require payroll deduction of union dues as a condition of employment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Unions, which would lose the legal ability to collect dues or fees from every worker they are required to represent, weakening their finances and bargaining strength. Workers who value union representation would bear the indirect cost: research on state right-to-work laws generally finds lower wages and weaker union coverage where such laws apply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unions and workers who rely on them

drawbacks.text: The bill lets a worker receive union representation — contract negotiation, grievance handling — without paying anything for it, which unions say forces them to spread their resources across non-contributors and gradually defunds representation [S2][S3].

State and national right-to-work laws are consistently associated in labor economics research with lower average wages and less union coverage, meaning workers who benefit from collective bargaining would likely bear the cost even if they never paid dues.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: individual freedom from compelled payment comes at the price of the collective fund that makes representation effective, and a workplace majority that voted for a union security agreement would no longer be able to enforce it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For an individual worker who objects to union fees, the bill offers a real, immediate gain. For the workforce as a whole, the mechanism it repeals is what funds union bargaining, and the preponderance of evidence on right-to-work laws points to lower wages where unions are weaker. The bill is a straightforward transfer of power from organized labor to individual workers and employers, and its net effect on ordinary workers depends heavily on whether they are inside a union or not.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up or reported it before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Coverdell introduced the bill on March 20, 1997, joined by Senator Faircloth [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S5].
Twenty-six Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the Congress ended in January 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unions kept the legal ability to negotiate union security agreements and collect dues from the workers they represent. Employers who wanted a national right-to-work law did not get one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Unions, which kept their dues authority

for.name: Sen. Paul Coverdell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered introductory remarks

for.name: National Right to Work Committee
for.what_they_did: Long championed a national right-to-work law of exactly this design and supported the bill's passage

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources (chaired by Sen. James Jeffords)
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; never scheduled the bill
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in the action history

sides.party_line_note: All 27 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans — including Coverdell, Faircloth, and 26 additional cosponsors — and no Democrat signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill repeals the legal foundation for union security agreements, cutting off dues and fees from workers unions must represent. Unions' ability to fund bargaining is the mechanism through which many workers' wages and benefits are set, so unions' stake here runs alongside the workers they represent.

industries.industry: Employers (general, especially unionized firms and railroads)
industries.note: Weaker union finances mean less bargaining power at the table, which tends to lower labor costs for employers. That gain comes directly out of the leverage workers exercise collectively.
The bill specifically repeals railroads' ability to require payroll deduction of union dues under the Railway Labor Act, removing an administrative mechanism and weakening rail unions' funding.
